نصلح الجيش؟» بل «أي دولة وأي أمن نريد؟» 29 أكتوبر، 2026 11:42 ص امستردام :28اكتوبر 2026م: راديو دبنقا خلص المنتدى الرابع ضمن سلسلة حوارية ينظمها «نداء سلام السودان» بتنسيق «مجموعة المناصرة من أجل السلام في السودان (AGPS)»، وعُقد في 22 أكتوبر 2026، إلى أن مستقبل القطاع الأمني والعسكري لا يُختزل في إصلاح الجيش، بل يتصل بطبيعة الدولة ومن يملك قرار استخدام القوة وكيف تخضع المؤسسات المسلحة للسلطة المدنية والقانون. ولم يحسم المنتدى الخلاف بين الخيارات المطروحة. حوار متعدد الخبرات وبحسب بيان مخرجات المنتدى الذى اطلع عليه راديو دبنقا والذى شارك فيه أكاديميون وباحثون وفاعلون مدنيون، إلى جانب ذوي خبرات عسكرية وشرطية وقضائية وحقوقية، وخبراء في التنمية والأمن القومي. أدار الحوار شمس الدين، وافتتحت أعماله الدكتورة أسماء النعيم والدكتور عصام عباس، وقدّم الدكتور لوكا بيونغ المساهمة الرئيسية، وشارك الدكتور فرانسيس دينغ في الافتتاح والختام. واستند النقاش إلى دراسة «تصورات السودانيين حول وقف الحرب والسلام»، التي وُصفت قراءاتها بأنها أولية وتحتاج إلى مراجعة قبل الاستشهاد بها. ومن مؤشراتها المعروضة أن 84.6% يرون أن تدخل العسكريين والأجهزة الأمنية في السياسة عائق أمام دولة مدنية ديمقراطية، وأن نحو 80% يحمّلون المؤسسة العسكرية وحلفاءها مسؤولية عالية عن النزاع. واختار 45.9% إعادة هيكلة شاملة، مقابل 37.5% فضّلوا الإصلاح عبر الدمج المتدرج، فيما أيّد 93.1% سلطة مدنية منتخبة وخاضعة للمساءلة. وبلغ مؤشر التوافق الإصلاحي 77.6% وطنياً، مع تفاوتات جغرافية. وأكد المنظمون أن تكرار رأي ما داخل المنتدى لا يقيس انتشاره بين السودانيين. الأمن شأن عام شددت المساهمة الرئيسية بحسب البيان على أن الأمن شأن عام لا يحتكر تعريفه العسكريون ولا ينحصر في حماية النظام، وأن على القوى المدنية صياغة رؤيتها لأمن البلاد قبل الجلوس إلى طاولة التفاوض، بدل ترك ذلك للأطراف المسلحة. وربطت بين التنمية والأمن، داعيةً إلى استراتيجية للأمن القومي تقوم على الأدلة والحوار مع المجتمع والمؤسسات. وأُشير إلى أن الجيش والشرطة والأجهزة الأمنية، حتى حين تُعد جزءاً من المشكلة، يمكن أن تكون جزءاً من الحل. واتسع النقاش ليشمل الشرطة والمخابرات والتشكيلات شبه العسكرية والميليشيات وعسكرة المجتمعات، مع التأكيد على اختلاف وظائف كل جهاز وضرورة معالجة كل مؤسسة على حدة. ثلاثة مسارات للخلاف ووفقا لبيان المنتدى برزت ثلاثة اتجاهات: الحل وإعادة التكوين، استناداً إلى تجارب دولية منها كوستاريكا، مع تحذيرات من فراغ أمني وانتشار الميليشيات؛ وإعادة البناء أو الإصلاح التحويلي العميق بالتدرج؛ والإصلاح المتدرج مع تغيير جذري في العقيدة والتركيبة والقيادة والرقابة. غير أن الحدود بين هذه الخيارات لم تكن ثابتة، إذ قبل بعض دعاة التغيير العميق التدرج، وطالب بعض المدافعين عن الإصلاح بتغيير جذري. وبقي السؤال الحاسم: كيف تستمر الوظائف الأمنية وحماية السكان أثناء الانتقال؟ واستُحضرت تجارب أجهزة الأمن في 1985 و2019، دون أن يقدم المنتدى رواية تاريخية نهائية بشأنها لاختلاف المشاركين في تقييمها. وقف الحرب أولاً أم الدولة المقبلة؟ أكدت البيان على ان مداخلات الترتيبات الأمنية في الهدنة، من مواقع انتشار القوات إلى حماية المدن ومراقبة الخروقات، تبدأ في تشكيل موازين القوة قبل اكتمال أي إصلاح. في المقابل، حذّر آخرون من أن تبتلع تصورات الدولة المقبلة أولوية وقف الحرب، وطالبوا العسكريين الحاليين والسابقين بالتحرك الآن لوقف القتال والحد من إنشاء الميليشيات. وظل الحد الأدنى الواجب تثبيته عند الهدنة بلا تحديد. حقوق مهنية لا امتيازات واشار البيان الى ان المشاركون ميزوا بين احتياجات الأفراد المشروعة، من أجور وسكن وتدريب ومستقبل مهني، وبين امتيازات القيادات الاقتصادية والسياسية. ورأى بعضهم أن تحسين أوضاع قاعدة المؤسسة يقلل قابلية توظيفها خلف طموحات القيادات، بينما حذّر آخرون من أن الطمأنة والحوافز لم تمنع في تجارب سابقة استعادة النفوذ. وفي يلى ملف الدمج،شدد المشاركون على طرح الاستيعاب الفردي وفق معايير مهنية بديلاً عن نقل تشكيلات كاملة بقياداتها ووالءاتها، خشية نقل المشكلة إلى داخل المؤسسة الموحدة. وأُشاروا إلى أن آلاف السودانيين والسودانيات أصبحوا مسلحين، وأن لحمل السلاح تاريخاً اجتماعياً في مناطق عدة، ما يتطلب بدائل أمنية وقانونية واقتصادية موثوقة. العدالة والمساءلة ووفقا للبيان رُبطت مداخلات حقوقية الإصلاح بالعدالة الانتقالية ومراجعة الحصانات وإدخال حقوق الإنسان في العقيدة والتدريب، ومنع التحاق من لهم سجل في الانتهاكات. وبقي مفتوحاً سؤال التوفيق بين إشراك أصحاب القوة المسلحة في وقف الحرب ومساءلتهم، إضافة إلى حماية النساء والناجين ومشاركتهم في تصميم الأمن. خيارات التنفيذ بلا قرار وتباينت المقترحات لحماية الانتقال:وراى المشاركون على ان حماية الانتقال تتم عبر التنظيم والضغط المدني، والحوار المدني العسكري، والإسناد الدولي، وقوة انتقالية متوافق عليها، وقيادة جماعية للمؤسسة العسكرية. وبحسب البيان لم يعتمد المنتدى أياً منها، مع التنبيه إلى أن أي قوة جديدة قد تعيد إنتاج مركز مسلح موازٍ ما لم تتضح تبعيتها وأساسها القانوني ورقابتها ومدتها. واختلف المشاركون كذلك في مسؤولية الانقلابات:حيث حمّل البعض القيادات العسكرية المبادرة بالاستيلاء على السلطة، ومن شدد على دور الأحزاب في استقطاب العسكريين وعلى أثر الأزمات الاقتصادية والانقسامات. ما لم يُحسم وما بعده لم يعتمد المنتدى نموذج إصلاح ولا خطة أمنية ولا نسبة دمج ولا هيكل قيادة ولا قوة جديدة، ولم يُسجَّل تصويت على أي منها. وأُعلن في الختام إعداد محضر وتقرير تحليلي وتوزيعهما، ومواصلة التواصل، والعمل على ورقة استراتيجية تُعرض للمراجعة، مع إتاحة بيانات الدراسة لمزيد من التقييم. وخلص التقرير بحسب البيان إلى أن أبرز ما أنجزه المنتدى هو إعادة تأطير النقاش: من شكل الجيش إلى علاقة السلاح بالسلطة والمجتمع، وربط ترتيبات وقف الحرب العاجلة بمستقبل السلطة المدنية والمؤسسات والمساءلة. إلى 188 قتيلاً و356 مصاباً، وفق أحدث إحصائية أعلنتها وزارة الصحة في حكومة "تأسيس"، التي يرأس مجلسها الرئاسي قائد قوات الدعم السريع محمد حمدان دقلو (حميدتي). وقالت الوزارة، في تحديث صادر من نيالا ، أمس الأربعاء، إن الحصيلة الجديدة تستند إلى التقارير الواردة من المؤسسات الصحية والفرق الطبية العاملة ميدانياً، موضحة أن أعداد الضحايا قد ترتفع مجدداً مع استمرار حصر القتلى والمصابين وتلقي البلاغات من المستشفيات والمرافق الصحية. وأضافت أن الكوادر الطبية والإسعافية تعمل تحت ضغوط استثنائية للتعامل مع الأعداد الكبيرة من الجرحى، وبينهم حالات خطيرة وحرجة تتطلب تدخلات جراحية عاجلة، في وقت تعاني فيه المؤسسات الصحية بنيالا نقصاً حاداً في الأدوية والمستلزمات الجراحية وأكياس الدم. وأكدت الوزارة أن الأرقام المعلنة تمثل الحصيلة المسجلة حتى وقت صدور تحديثها الأخير، مطالبة المنظمات الدولية والإنسانية بالتدخل العاجل لدعم مستشفيات نيالا، وتوفير الإمدادات الطبية اللازمة لإنقاذ حياة المصابين. وكانت مجموعة " محامو الطوارئ " قد قالت إن المسيّرة قصفت السوق مساء الاثنين، مخلّفةً، وفق حصيلة أولية، عشرات القتلى والمصابين، بينهم نساء وأطفال. ووصفت المجموعة الهجوم بأنه " مجزرة " حوّلت سوقاً مكتظة بالمدنيين، يقصدها السكان لتأمين احتياجاتهم اليومية وكسب أرزاقهم، إلى ساحة للقتل والإصابات الجماعية. وحمّلت القوات المسلحة السودانية مسؤولية الهجوم، مطالبةً بإجراء تحقيق مستقل وشفاف، وتحديد المسؤولين عنه ومحاسبتهم. وتعزز إفادة مستقلة لمنظمة " أطباء بلا حدود " وقوع الهجوم ونسبته إلى الجيش السوداني؛ إذ قالت المنظمة إن مسيّرة تابعة للجيش ضربت سوقاً مزدحماً غربي نيالا نحو الساعة الثامنة من مساء 26 أكتوبر، قبل أن تضرب غارة ثانية حياً سكنياً. ووصلت إلى مستشفى نيالا التعليمي، الذي تدعمه المنظمة، جثامين 36 شخصاً، كان 21 منهم يرتدون ملابس مدنية، بينما عالجت الفرق الطبية أكثر من 150 مصاباً، بينهم نساء وأطفال يعانون إصابات بالشظايا وحروقاً خطيرة. ولا تمثل أرقام "أطباء بلا حدود" حصيلة شاملة للهجوم، لأنها تقتصر على الضحايا الذين وصلوا إلى مستشفى نيالا التعليمي، بينما قالت وزارة الصحة التابعة لحكومة "تأسيس" إن إحصائيتها الأوسع جُمعت من المؤسسات الصحية والفرق الميدانية المختلفة. وأدانت الوزارة ما وصفته باستهداف المدنيين والأسواق والمنشآت المدنية، مؤكدة أن حماية السكان وضمان وصول الجرحى إلى الخدمات الصحية التزامان أساسيان بموجب القانون الدولي الإنساني. كما طالبت بتحقيق مستقل ومحاسبة المسؤولين عن الهجوم وضمان عدم إفلات مرتكبيه من العقاب. وتحول سوق " تنقونج "، الذي يقصده السكان للحصول على الغذاء والاحتياجات اليومية، إلى ساحة مكتظة بالجثامين والمصابين، في مجزرة جديدة تضاف إلى سجل الضربات الجوية التي نفذها الجيش السوداني على الأسواق والأحياء السكنية في دارفور ومناطق أخرى من البلاد. ولم يتسنَّ التحقق بصورة مستقلة من الحصيلة النهائية التي أعلنتها حكومة "تأسيس"، فيما قالت وكالة أسوشيتد برس إن صعوبة الوصول إلى نيالا تعرقل التحقق الميداني من عدد الضحايا. غير أن الثابت سقوط مدنيين ووقوع الهجوم على سوق مزدحم ما يعيد طرح الأسئلة بشأن نمط استخدام الجيش للمسيّرات في مناطق مكتظة، والكلفة البشرية المتصاعدة لحرب يدفع المدنيون ثمنها الأكبر. وتثير الحصيلة الضخمة، إلى جانب توقيت الهجوم وطبيعة الموقع، أسئلة جدية بشأن اختيار الهدف والذخيرة المستخدمة، ومدى التزام قيادة الجيش بمبادئ التمييز والتناسب واتخاذ الاحتياطات التي يفرضها القانون الدولي الإنساني. كما تعزز الضربتان المطالب بإخضاع عمليات المسيّرات التابعة للجيش لتحقيق دولي مستقل، وحفظ الأدلة الرقمية والطبية، وتحديد الجهة التي نفذت الهجمات على المدنيين، وقيادة الوحدة التي اختارت الأهداف وأصدرت أوامر القصف. مجزرة سوق تنقونج هي هجوم دموي آخر على موقع مدني معروف، سبقته ضربة مماثلة على سوق المواشي في المدينة نفسها. وعندما تتحول الأسواق التي يبحث فيها الناس عن الطعام والرزق إلى أهداف متكررة، تصبح قيادة القوات المسلحة السودانية مطالبة بالإجابة في تحقيق أمام لجان التحقيق الدولية وبعثات تقصي الحقائق، لا بالاكتفاء بالصمت أو بالادعاء العام باستهداف مواقع عسكرية. أخبار السودان الجيش السوداني تأسيس الحرب في السودان نيالا طائرات مسيرة عاجل l أبو ظبي - سكاي نيوز عربية {{::article.mediaAsset.caption}} {{article.match.competition}} - والوقود في أم درمان والمناقل وهيا. وشملت المواقع المستهدفة، بحسب المجموعة، محطة المرخيات التحويلية في أم درمان، ومحطة الكهرباء الرئيسية بمدينة المناقل في ولاية الجزيرة، إلى جانب مستودعات للوقود وخط نحو 13 محطة، معتبرةً أن هذه الهجمات تفاقم التداعيات الإنسانية للحرب وتقوض مقومات الحياة. وحمّلت المجموعة قوات الدعم السريع مسؤولية الهجمات، مطالبةً بوقف استهداف البنية التحتية المدنية والتحقيق في والإفلات من العقاب شجّع على ارتكاب المزيد من الجرائم منذ 9 ساعات عبد الحميد صيام حجم الخط 0 الأمم المتحدة- «القدس العربي»: في مؤتمر صحافي للجنة التحقيق المستقلة في السودان، قال رئيس اللجنة محمد شاندي عثمان، يوم الأربعاء، إن المدنيين في مدينة الأبيض بالسودان يعيشون في حالة من الخوف الدائم جراء هجمات الطائرات المسيّرة التي تشنها قوات الدعم السريع ، وموجة الاعتقالات التعسفية التي تنفذها القوات المسلحة السودانية. وحذّر المحققون من أن الحرب تتوسع جغرافياً وتزداد تعقيداً من الناحية التكنولوجية، كما أصبحت تشكل خطراً متزايداً على المدنيين. وقالت منى رشماوي، وهي خبيرة في البعثة الدولية المستقلة لتقصي الحقائق بشأن السودان، خلال مؤتمر صحافي: «لقد اعتقلت الأجهزة الأمنية التابعة للقوات المسلحة السودانية آلاف الأشخاص، واحتجزتهم وعرّضتهم للتعذيب في أماكن احتجاز غير رسمية وفي سجن الأبيض المركزي، في ظل ظروف مروعة». وأضافت: «يجب أن تتوقف هذه الممارسات فوراً». وقد أصدرت البعثة تقريرها الجديد، الذي يحمل عنوان «حرب السودان المتواصلة: دمار يلحق بالمدنيين وتفاقم انعدام الأمن في الأبيض»، وذلك عقب عرض نتائج توصلت إليها في أيلول/سبتمبر حول الدعم الخارجي للأطراف المتحاربة أمام اللجنة الثالثة للجمعية العامة للأمم المتحدة. وحول تقرير البعثة الدولية، التي شكّلها مجلس حقوق الإنسان، قال عثمان إن البعثة وجدت أسباباً معقولة للاعتقاد بأن النقل الخارجي للأسلحة والتكنولوجيا العسكرية والدعم اللوجستي والأفراد الأجانب عزّز القدرات العسكرية لكلا الطرفين، ويسّر الاستخدام المتزايد لأنظمة الأسلحة المعقدة، وخاصة المسيّرات بعيدة المدى. ودعا عثمان الأطراف التي تغذي الصراع بالأسلحة والمقاتلين والمساعدات العسكرية، والمنتفعين اقتصادياً منه، إلى إعادة النظر في عواقب أفعالها واحترام القانون الدولي. وأضاف أن تلك التطورات توسع النطاق الجغرافي للصراع وتزيد المخاطر على المدنيين. وقال: «وجدنا أيضاً أسباباً معقولة للاعتقاد بأن شبكة عابرة للدول تعمل عبر عدة بلدان، مكّنت وعزّزت العمليات العسكرية لقوات الدعم السريع. الأدلة التي جمعتها البعثة تشير إلى تورط أفراد وجهات تعمل من دولة الإمارات العربية المتحدة، وتشاد، وجنوب شرق ليبيا، وبونتلاند بالصومال، يسّروا نقل أسلحة وتكنولوجيا مرتبطة بالمسيّرات ودعم لوجستي وأفراد إلى مناطق تسيطر عليها قوات الدعم السريع، بما فيها نيالا بولاية جنوب دارفور». وذكر رئيس الفريق، عثمان، أن مسؤولية الدول تتجاوز حدودها، داعياً من يفاقمون الصراع ويستفيدون منه اقتصادياً إلى إعادة النظر في عواقب أفعالهم، وإلى احترام القانون الدولي. وقال: «مع ارتكاب فظائع بشكل يومي في السودان، من الواضح أن مستقبل الشعب لا يمكن أن يُبنى على أساس الإفلات من العقاب». وشدّد على ضرورة ألا تقتصر المساءلة على الجناة فقط، بل أن تشمل أيضاً ممولي وميسري ارتكاب الجرائم. وأكد أن إرساء مسار لتحقيق السلام العادل والدائم في السودان يحتم توفير الحماية وضمان منع وقوع الانتهاكات والمساءلة عنها. ورداً على أسئلة «القدس العربي» حول دور المجتمع المدني الذي ساهم في إسقاط نظام عمر البشير، قالت جوي إنغيزو إيزيللو، عضوة الفريق، إن الفضاء المدني في السودان قد تقلص كثيراً. وأضافت: «كثير منهم غادر البلاد أو انتهى به الأمر في السجون، ولم يعد لهم دور يُذكر، وهو ما أشرنا إليه في التقرير. ولكن بقي بعض المدافعين عن حقوق الإنسان وبعض النشطاء الذين يحاولون أن يتجمعوا، ولكنهم يخشون، إن قالوا شيئاً، أن يُصنّفوا مع هذا الطرف أو ذاك. والهجوم عليهم يعرقل جهود الفريق في توثيق عمل المنظمات المدنية». وقالت: «نحن نصرّ في كل مداولاتنا على ضم هذه العناصر للمحادثات، بمن فيهم النساء اللواتي يتعرضن لحزمة من الانتهاكات. التضامن الدولي يجب أن يكون مع المجتمع المدني السوداني، لا مع حملة السلاح». ورداً على سؤال ثانٍ لـ«القدس العربي» حول دور الدول الأخرى المجاورة للسودان، وخاصة إثيوبيا ومصر وتشاد، قال رئيس الفريق محمد عثمان: «إن التحقيقات ما زالت جارية لمعرفة أدوار الدول المجاورة الأخرى. نتواصل مع تشاد. هم ينكرون التدخل، ولكن لدينا وثائق تثبت أن لهم دوراً في النزاع، ولكننا نتحاور معهم ونرحب باستعدادهم للحوار معنا، وخاصة أن لديهم عدداً كبيراً من اللاجئين». وأضافت السيدة منى رشماوي أن حدود السودان ملتهبة الآن، وخاصة من إثيوبيا، وهناك حادث مواجهة مع مصر. وكلما تضعضع وضع السودان، تأثرت دول الجوار. والسودان لديه حدود واسعة مع إثيوبيا وتشاد. وقالت رشماوي: «هناك مشكلة إضافية، وهي وجود مرتزقة من كولومبيا. نتحاور مع الدولة الكولومبية الآن لإيجاد مخرج لمسألة المرتزقة. الوضع في السودان معقد كثيراً». ورداً على سؤال متابعة لـ«القدس العربي» حول تحول ميليشيا الجنجويد إلى قوات التدخل السريع، وكيف خدع عمر البشير الأمم المتحدة عندما غيّر الاسم، ثم جرى دمج الميليشيا في الجيش، وفي أول فرصة سنحت لها للانشقاق، انسحبت من الجيش تحت اسم قوات التدخل السريع، ردّ عثمان: «نعم، هذا صحيح. لقد تمت شرعنة الجنجويد بعد عام 2005، ولكنهم انفصلوا بعد عام 2023. الشيء المهم هو أنه لم تكن هناك مساءلة منذ أن كانوا جنجويد وحتى الآن. لم تتم مساءلة أحد. يجب أن تكون هناك آلية لمحاسبة المتهمين بحرب الإبادة. يجب أن تكون هناك مساءلة الآن ليصبحوا نموذجاً لردع غيرهم». كلمات مفتاحية عبد الحميد صيام الأمم المتحدة الحرب في السودان قوات الدعم الحرب الدائرة في بلاده، دون أن يسمي أيا منها. ووفقا لوكالة الأنباء السودانية (سونا) أكد كبرون أن أكثر من 20 دولة تشارك في الحرب الدائرة في السودان عبر "الدعم اللوجيستي والمرتزقة والمال والمسيرات لقوات أسبوع end of list وقال إن ما يجري في السودان ليس حربا أهلية أو صراعا على السلطة، بل حرب شاملة تستهدف تدمير البلاد ونهب ثرواتها وتغيير ديمغرافيتها. حطام مسيّرة جرى عرضه خلال مؤتمر صحفي بالخرطوم (الجزيرة) في السياق نفسه، اتهم وكيل وزارة الخارجية السودانية معاوية عثمان خالد إثيوبيا بدعم قوات الدعم السريع عسكريا ولوجستيا. وقال خالد -في مؤتمر صحفي مشترك للدفاع والخارجية والإعلام والاستخبارات في الخرطوم- إن كل المسيّرات التي استهدفت محطات الطاقة والكهرباء والأعيان المدنية والمرافق الحيوية خلال الأيام الماضية انطلقت من الأراضي الإثيوبية. من جانبه، قال المتحدث باسم الجيش العميد عصام عوض إن الفترة الماضية شهدت انطلاق 162 هجوما بالمسيّرات من أراضي إثيوبيا، أدت إلى مقتل أكثر من 400 مدني، و102 من العسكريين. أدلة على تورط إثيوبيا وذكر وكيل وزارة الخارجية السودانية خلال المؤتمر الصحفي أن الأدلة تثبت دعم أديس أبابا قوات الدعم السريع بالسلاح وتجنيد المرتزقة ومنصات إطلاق الطائرات المسيرة. وقال إن بلاده تمتلك أدلة تثبت أن جميع الطائرات المسيرة التي استهدفت السودان مؤخرا انطلقت من دولة إثيوبيا . وأكد وكيل الخارجية السودانية أن السودان يحتفظ بحق الرد على إثيوبيا، مشيرا إلى أن الأجهزة العسكرية والأمنية قادرة على حماية البلاد. كما طالب المجتمع الدولي باتخاذ خطوات ملموسة و"ترك الصمت" لوقف الاعتداءات على السودان. استهداف المؤسسات الحيوية وفي هذا السياق قال وكيل وزارة الثقافة والإعلام السوداني جراهام عبد القادر إن "مليشيا الدعم السريع استهدفت المؤسسات الحيوية بالطائرات المسيرة، لا سيما محطات الكهرباء، في عدة ولايات شملت النيل الأزرق والنيل الأبيض والخرطوم و الجزيرة والقضارف". إعلان ولفت عبد القادر إلى أن قوات الدعم السريع تسعى عبر استهدافها المؤسسات الحيوية في السودان إلى منع المواطنين من العودة إلى منازلهم. وشدد وكيل وزارة الثقافة والإعلام على أن السودان لطالما استخدم مبدأ "الصبر الإستراتيجي" في التعامل مع ما وصفه بـ"العدوان الإثيوبي". وعلى مدار 8 أيام، كثفت قوات الدعم السريع هجماتها بطائرات مسيرة على 7 محطات كهرباء في عدد من الولايات بالسودان، آخرها محطة المرخيات في أم درمان التي تعرضت لهجوم صباح أمس الثلاثاء. وشملت الهجمات كذلك محطتي تندلتي ومشكور في ولاية النيل الأبيض، والحواتة والفاو بولاية القضارف، والجنيد في ولاية الجزيرة، وسنجة ب ولاية سنار ، في أحدث واقعة أبلغ عنها مصدر حكومي للجزيرة صباح اليوم. المصدر: الجزيرة + وكالات aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo إعلان من ethiopia.title: Former PM Hailemariam Says Ethiopia's Pursuit of Sea Access Rational
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Former PM Hailemariam Says Ethiopia's Pursuit of Sea Access Rational - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Former PM Hailemariam Says Ethiopia's Pursuit of Sea Access Rational 29 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia's pursuit of sustainable sea access is a rational and undeniable national aspiration that should be addressed through dialogue and negotiations, former Prime Minister Hailemariam Desalegn said. In an exclusive interview with ENA, Hailemariam said the central question should not be whether Ethiopia needs access to the sea, but how the country can secure it peacefully through mutually beneficial arrangements. He noted that Ethiopia, with a population of about 130 million, a growing economy and a vast land area, is the world's most populous landlocked country. He described the loss of direct maritime access as a historical scar that continues to shape the country's economic and strategic interests. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The former premier also questioned the geographical circumstances that have left Ethiopia without direct access to the Red Sea despite its proximity, saying the issue deserves serious consideration. He traced the current regional arrangement to the European scramble for Africa in the 1880s, arguing that leaving the matter unresolved would pass the challenge from one generation to the next. According to the him, history, geography, culture and law are important considerations in discussions about Ethiopia's maritime interests, particularly the role of sea access in trade, economic development and regional integration. He further urged neighboring countries to view Ethiopia's aspirations in the context of shared economic growth, peace and security, emphasizing the need to find a solution that serves the interests of the region and future generations. "Access to a sea outlet should be viewed as a crucial catalyst for joint regional development", he stressed, calling for constructive discussions to find a mutually beneficial solution. Hailemariam also warned that opposition to Ethiopia's maritime aspirations stems from a malicious intent to undermine the country's anchor role and regional power status. Drawing a parallel to past regional tensions, he recalled how Egypt previously argued that filling the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam would severely harm downstream interests and demanded a 20-year timeline, only for the filling to be successfully completed in four years while Egypt ultimately received more water. Stakeholders should face the sea-access issue realistically and pursue a peaceful solution that supports shared development and regional stability rather than act out of unfounded fears, he concluded with a traditional proverb: "A dog chased by a hyena by moonlight will not venture outside by day." ethiopia.content: Ethiopia receives 12 Russian Su-35 jets, plans S-400 acquisition - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY Ethiopia receives 12 Russian Su-35 jets, plans S-400 acquisition Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Faisal Ali Thursday October 29, 2026 Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed holds a framed certificate alongside officials in front of a fighter jet in an image shared on his X account on October 28, 2026 [Handout/Abiy Ahmed] Ethiopia has received 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets and will also acquire four S-400 air defence batteries, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced. Abiy made the announcement on X on Wednesday during a visit to Moscow for the two-day Russia-Africa Summit, where Russia is seeking closer security and economic ties with African countries. The acquisition comes as Ethiopian forces fight renewed battles with rebels in northern Tigray and a separate rebellion in the neighbouring Amhara region. advertisements The prime minister said the warplanes had arrived a year earlier than expected under an existing agreement with Moscow, thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin for helping speed up the delivery. He gave no date for the arrival of the S-400 batteries, designed to shoot down aircraft and missiles. Abiy said on Wednesday that the new equipment would strengthen Ethiopia’s ability to “preemptively deter aggression”. In a second X post later that day, he described the jets as newly deployed and said they would defend Ethiopian airspace. Military cooperation The announcement is the latest sign of Russia‘s growing military partnership with Ethiopia, following a series of agreements in recent years. The two governments signed a military cooperation agreement in Addis Ababa in July 2021 aimed at improving the Ethiopian armed forces’ training and technology. In January, defence publication Janes reported that Ethiopia had displayed newly acquired Russian Yak-130 advanced jet trainers during celebrations marking its air force’s 90th anniversary. Russia supplied 15 percent of Africa’s imports of major weapons between 2021 and 2025, making it the continent’s third-largest supplier, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. Moscow has sought closer military and economic ties with African countries while facing Western sanctions over its war in Ukraine. The Russia-Africa Summit, which began on Wednesday, brings African leaders together for talks on trade, investment and security. Tigray war The announcement follows a major shift in the fighting in Tigray, where government troops and allied forces entered the regional capital Mekelle on October 4 after fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) withdrew. The TPLF, an armed group that previously governed the region, has suffered further territorial losses as government forces advanced into other towns. Addis Ababa has since appointed a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray, but the fighting has not stopped. A TPLF commander called for continued resistance in a television broadcast last week, while the group has also claimed attacks against government-aligned troops in northwestern Tigray on Wednesday. The renewed war has effectively undone a peace agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in November 2022 that ended two years of fighting, which researchers at Belgium’s Ghent University estimate killed about 500,000 civilians. Government forces are also battling Fano, an Amhara armed group that has been fighting federal troops since 2023. ethiopia.content: Stakeholder-led nutrition interventions fall short in Eastern Ethiopia, HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, October 29, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Stakeholder-led nutrition interventions fall short in Eastern Ethiopia, survey finds by October 29, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Stakeholder-led nutrition interventions fall short in Eastern Ethiopia, survey finds Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram A new study of rural households in Eastern Ethiopia finds that despite a wide range of stakeholder-led nutrition security interventions, the average household dietary diversity score in the study area was 4.02, well below the national household dietary diversity score of 5.42. Half of the sampled households fell into the category of low dietary diversity, according to the survey results published in BMC Nutrition. The study was led by Mideksa Fufa Jilito, Fekadu Beyene Kenee, Andreas Thiel and Chanyalew Seyoum Aweke, and examined how stakeholders’ interventions relate to the nutrition of rural households. The authors note that Ethiopia’s government has been implementing several initiatives and policies to address nutrition problems, yet nutrition problems continue to affect the country’s socioeconomic and health circumstances. For the household component, the researchers digitally collected primary data from 385 randomly selected households. In addition to the household survey, they gathered data from stakeholders to examine their contributions to households’ nutrition security, purposively selecting 84 stakeholder employees for that survey. To analyse the household data, the team applied a generalized ordered logit model to estimate factors associated with households’ nutritional status. Stakeholder data was analysed separately using descriptive analysis to complement the household data. The survey of stakeholders revealed that several organisations intervene in both the production and consumption of nutrient-dense crops. Their reported mechanisms include training, seed delivery, and home-garden-based vegetable production, indicating a broad portfolio of activities aimed at improving what rural households grow and eat. The econometric model results showed that access to extension services, irrigation facilities, and engaging women in farming activities were positively associated with the medium and high nutritional status of rural households. These associations suggest that households with better access to agricultural support and water infrastructure, and those where women participate in farming, tended to be represented more in the higher nutritional status categories. By contrast, several factors were negatively correlated with the medium and high nutritional status of households. These included the sex of the household head, credit services, market distance, healthcare services, and changes in weather variability. The study reports these as correlations from the model, not as experimentally established causal effects. The authors conclude that relevant stakeholders working on agriculture and nutrition interventions should pay attention to take action on nutrition-related concerns in Eastern Ethiopia. The finding that the local average dietary diversity score sits below the national figure, with half of sampled households in the low diversity category, underscores the gap between the range of interventions described by stakeholders and the measured nutritional status of households in the study area. As an observational study based on a cross-sectional household survey and descriptive stakeholder analysis, the research describes associations within the sampled population rather than testing the effectiveness of specific interventions. The article was published on 29 October 2026 as an open access research paper in BMC Nutrition, and is currently shared as an accepted manuscript that remains subject to further edits before the final Version of Record. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia receives 12 Russian fighter jets and air defence systems as Tigray war escalates Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Ethiopia acquires Russian fighter jets and air defence systems amid war in Tigray 4 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Basillioh Rukanga and Michael Teferi , BBC Africa Abiy Ahmed/Facebook The acquisition of fighter jets comes amid ongoing tensions with Eritrea Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, as fighting intensified in the northern Tigray region neighbouring Eritrea. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who is attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, described the acquisition as a "milestone" that would boost Ethiopia's defence capacity. He said Ethiopia and Russia agreed on the deal several years ago and the warplanes had come ahead of schedule. He also said that Ethiopia had plans to acquire four S-400 air defence systems from Moscow. The Ethiopian leader said the military hardware was essential to protect the country from external threats. Abiy, who described Russian President Vladimir Putin, "as a close friend of Ethiopia", said Ethiopia had now become the first country in sub‑Saharan Africa to own this kind of "advanced combat technology." "If we fail to build this capability, surviving as a country in our region will become difficult. Countries with sufficient preparation are not easily defied," he said. Russia and Ethiopia have signed several military agreements in recent years, including a deal in 2021 to train and improve technology for the military. Abiy explained that Ethiopia signed an agreement with Russia several years ago to procure the Su‑35 jets and S‑400 systems, citing global air force trends and security threats facing the country. The Su‑35, he noted, is equipped for both air‑to‑air and air‑to‑ground combat, with the ability to detect and neutralize incoming cruise missiles at distances of up to 200 kilometers. Military intelligence analyst Qalaab Segatu told BBC Amharic that Ethiopia's acquisition of additional warplanes was a key indication that "it was preparing for possible wars with other countries, not just internal conflicts". According to him, the jets are highly maneuverable and capable of covering large areas, with radars capable of ensuring air superiority and long-range scanning. When combined, the fighter jets and air defence systems "create a significant capability to protect and defend major cities and critical infrastructure such as the Renaissance Dam, providing key strategic air superiority," Qalaab said. Abiy said besides the advanced capabilities of the aircraft from Russia, the use of drones was equally important in strengthening deterrence. Ethiopia has extensively used military drones, including those sourced from Turkey and China, in recent conflicts. "We need to build capacity not only with drones, but also with the fourth generation capabilities of the Su 30 and Su 35 [aircraft]," Abiy said. The latest acquisition of military hardware from Russia comes after the current conflict in northern Tigray started last month between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which it denies. Tensions between the two countries have also persisted as Abiy terms Ethiopia's lack of direct sea access an "existential question", which Eritrea views as a direct threat to its sovereignty. Eritrea gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long war with Ethiopia, with the latter losing access to the sea. ethiopia.content: How Is Washington Positioning Itself Amid Ethiopia’s Security Challenges? – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-29 How Is Washington Positioning Itself Amid Ethiopia’s Security Challenges? 0 Comments Asked about the risk of war between Ethiopia and Eritrea, Rubio said that “separatists” had attacked inside Ethiopia, that Ethiopia had responded and that troops were now “surging on both sides of the border.” He warned that this could become “a broader conflict” and “pull in other countries.” He also described the reported attacks by the “separatists” as terrorist attacks, while urging Ethiopia to respond “wise[ly] and measured[ly].” In his call with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed days ago, he had framed the situation far more conventionally. He called for de-escalation by all sides, dialogue under the 2018 Ethiopia-Eritrea peace framework, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity and an end to cross-border incursions. The timing coincides with the escalating confrontation between the federal government and the TPLF, as well as rising tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea. By framing their activities in terms of separatism and terrorism, Washington moved beyond its earlier emphasis on conflict management toward a more explicit political distinction between the Ethiopian government and those challenging its authority. It marked a notable change in American public characterization of the conflict in Ethiopia since the northern conflict. At the same time, the United States indicated that it was gradually reopening diplomatic channels with Eritrea, so that it would have enough standing to speak to both sides and ease tensions. The shift in Washington’s public messaging was also reflected in its response to the TPLF months ago. In his September statement following the TPLF’s seizure of airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire and the outbreak of renewed fighting, U.S. Ambassador Ervin Massinga said the TPLF leadership had made the “poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive.” He accused it of engaging in an “unwinnable fight,” criticized its rejection of AU-sponsored dialogue, and warned that the United States could impose further sanctions. Earlier in June, the State Department also imposed targeted visa restrictions on TPLF officials it accused of ‘undermining resolution to the crisis in Tigray. The terrorism label Rubio has framed could strengthen the Ethiopian government’s hand. Ethiopia’s parliament had itself listed the TPLF as a terrorist group during the northern conflict in 2021, and formally lifted the designation only when it removed the group from the national list as part of implementing the Pretoria peace agreement. For the alliance, designation and isolation could also become a means of fracturing the coalition, particularly if followed by targeted sanctions, in addition to their unresolved tensions and lack of clarity surrounding the relationships among its constituent groups. The timing of US measures reinforces this interpretation. Washington lifted restrictions on defense exports to Ethiopia in February, followed by the termination of the sanctions regime established under Executive Order 14046 on September. The latter brought an end to the associated sanctions and removed the designated individuals and entities from the U.S. sanctions list, signaling a broader adjustment in American policy toward both Ethiopia and Eritrea. These moves are consistent with a long-standing American strategic interest in a stable Ethiopia capable of contributing to regional security, an objective explicitly articulated in the State Department’s 2023 country strategy . Although the current administration’s approach differs in important respects from that of its predecessor, the underlying strategic interest remains relevant to understanding Washington’s calculations in the Horn of Africa. Meanwhile, as Washington recalibrates its approach to the Horn of Africa in response to shifting strategic priorities, it has moved to reopen relations with Eritrea including through sanctions relief and renewed diplomatic contact. The timing has become particularly significant as the risk of direct confrontation between Ethiopia and Eritrea has intensified, placing Washington’s engagement with Asmara within a much more consequential regional security context. Rubio’s subsequent remarks made clear that the administration views these channels as necessary to preserve its ability to engage both sides and potentially mediate the dispute. The recent developments and Rubio’s words suggest that Washington might appear to be pursuing four overlapping objectives. It wants to prevent a wider interstate war that could draw in additional actors and disrupt Red Sea shipping. Simultaneously, taken from Rubio’s words, it seems to back Ethiopia’s territorial integrity and its right to counter armed challenges framed as separatism or terrorism. On the other hand, it wants to keep just enough engagement with Eritrea for communication and Red Sea positioning. And it wants to protect and expand commercial footholds that reward a functional Ethiopian center. Washington’s approach reflects an effort to manage the immediate risks of escalation while preserving strategic flexibility in a region where its interests increasingly overlap and sometimes conflict. However, given Eritrea’s longstanding pattern of regional behavior, the expectation that diplomatic outreach alone can moderate its conduct remains difficult to sustain. The effectiveness of Washington’s approach will ultimately depend on whether renewed engagement can translate into concrete changes in Asmara’s regional calculations, particularly its role in Ethiopia’s internal conflict and its willingness to reduce the risk of interstate escalation. Besides, the diplomatic reset comes amid intensified concerns over Eritrea’s role in Ethiopia’s internal conflict, with sanctions relief coinciding with the formation of the Alliance for Survival and reports of Eritrean forces advancing tens of kilometers into Ethiopian territory, raising risks of interstate confrontation. However, rather than steering Asmara away from a proxy strategy, American engagement appears to have changed very little. Contacts between American and Eritrean officials have continued even as Eritrea’s backing for the TPLF and the broader rebel coalition has become more visible. Eritrea’s public narrative sits uneasily with its conduct on the ground. Asmara appears to be employing a victimhood narrative to portray Eritrea as the aggrieved party, attribute the escalating confrontation to Ethiopia and divert international scrutiny from its own conduct. Sophia Tesfamariam’s recent diplomatic outreach appears consistent with this effort to shape international perceptions in Eritrea’s favor. Meanwhile, Eritrean forces remain on Ethiopian territory, it continues to support armed proxies inside Ethiopia and its actions appear consistent with an effort to establish strategic depth through a buffer along the frontier. This pattern is difficult to reconcile with a purely defensive posture or Asmara’s portrayal of Eritrea as the aggrieved party. It also raises questions about the central assumption underlying Washington’s approach in that diplomatic engagement can moderate Eritrea’s behavior despite evidence and behavior pointing in the opposite direction. Rubio’s characterization of the attackers as separatists, coupled with Eritrea’s support for these forces, could complicate Asmara’s efforts to sustain its victimhood narrative. The contradiction between portraying Eritrea as the aggrieved party and supporting armed groups challenging its federal authority would undermine Eritrea’s effort to present itself as the victim. For a state that has long approached regional politics through strategic suspicion, confrontation and the cultivation of leverage through neighboring conflicts, renewed diplomatic standing may not necessarily translate into restraint. It also has the risk to simply give Eritrea more room to pursue its regional objectives. Washington’s interest in Eritrea is shaped by the strategic importance of the Bab el-Mandeb and the vulnerability of Red Sea shipping. Even so, Isaias Afwerki’s longstanding skepticism toward Washington reinforced by years of hostility, accusations and Eritrea’s adversarial posture toward US regional policy, raises serious questions about whether renewed diplomatic engagement can overcome the mistrust that has long defined their relationship. Additionally, Asmara has kept closer ties with Iran has shown little enthusiasm for confronting the Houthis and was absent from the Saudi-led coalition formed to counter them. Engagement may give Washington a diplomatic channel to Asmara, but Eritrea’s unpredictable regional posture raises the risk that renewed American recognition could embolden its leadership without securing any meaningful restraint. Rubio’s repeated emphasis on preventing a conflict that “could ultimately pull in other countries” is both a warning and an acknowledgment of regional entanglement. A purely bilateral containment strategy risks underestimating how actions in one theater alter the cost-benefit calculations in another. Washington’s renewed engagement could create an opening to press Eritrea toward restraint and reduce the risk of interstate conflict. Whether that opportunity produces a more stable relationship will depend on whether diplomatic access is accompanied by credible pressure and measurable changes in Asmara’s conduct. ethiopia.content: Sudan Once Again Accuses Ethiopia of Involvement in Drone Strikes Targeting Power Stations, Civilian Sites - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Sudan Once Again Accuses Ethiopia of Involvement in Drone Strikes Targeting Power Stations, Civilian Sites 29 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Sudan has once again accused neighbouring Ethiopia of involvement in drone attacks targeting civilian infrastructure, fuel depots and power stations, alleging that drones used in recent strikes were launched from Ethiopian territory, including Bahir Dar Airport. According to Sudan Tribune , Sudanese government and intelligence officials made the allegations at a joint press conference in Khartoum on Wednesday, presenting what they described as flight data, satellite imagery and fragments of intercepted drones to support their claims. The accusations followed a series of strikes on Sudanese infrastructure. On Tuesday, a drone attack disabled the Markhiyat power station northwest of Omdurman, disrupting electricity supplies across the capital area. Further strikes on Wednesday targeted a power station and fuel storage facilities in El Manaqil, Gezira State, as well as fuel storage sites and a pipeline linked to Bashayer Port in Red Sea State. Sudanese officials accused Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of enabling the attacks. Undersecretary of Foreign Affairs Muawiya Osman Khalid called on the international community to respond to what he described as Ethiopian-Emirati aggression, while asserting Sudan's right to defend its territory. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Ethiopian authorities and the UAE could not immediately be reached for comment. The flight data and the alleged origin of the drones could not be independently verified. The allegations came as Sudan's Defence Minister Hassan Daoud Kabroun accused more than 20 countries of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) with funding, drones, logistical assistance and foreign fighters, according to a separate report by Radio Tamazuj. In an interview published Wednesday by the state-run Sudan News Agency, Kabroun did not identify the countries beyond repeating allegations against Ethiopia and the UAE. He provided no evidence for his latest claims. The UAE has denied supporting the RSF. Sudan's army and the RSF have been fighting since April 2023, when tensions over plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the regular military escalated into war. Kabroun also called for renewed regional security cooperation, including joint border protection and arrangements to strengthen maritime security along Sudan's Red Sea coastline. ethiopia.title: Uganda Embassy in Addis Ababa Backs IACO's New AU Office, Continental Coffee Strategy
ethiopia.content: Africa: Uganda Embassy in Addis Ababa Backs IACO's New AU Office, Continental Coffee Strategy - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Uganda Embassy in Addis Ababa Backs IACO's New AU Office, Continental Coffee Strategy 28 October 2026 The Independent (Kampala) Addis Ababa, Ethiopia — The Uganda Embassy in Addis Ababa has expressed strong support for the Inter-African Coffee Organisation (IACO) and its newly opened office at the African Union headquarters, reaffirming Uganda's commitment to a continental strategy aimed at transforming Africa's coffee sector. The support was conveyed during a courtesy call on the Chargé d'Affaires a.i. at the Uganda Embassy, Margaret Kafeero, by Ambassador Solomon Rutega, Secretary-General of IACO. The high-level meeting focused on IACO's expanding institutional footprint in Addis Ababa and the joint execution of a historic framework to overhaul the African coffee industry. During the briefing, Ambassador Rutega outlined the structural changes underway following the 37th AU Summit, where the African Union officially adopted coffee as a strategic anchor commodity--a landmark policy shift that fully endorses the Kampala Declaration originally drafted by the G25 African coffee-producing nations. "We are entering an era of aggressive restructuring to fundamentally alter global trade dynamics," Ambassador Rutega said. "While the global coffee sector generates over $465 billion annually, African producing countries currently receive less than $3 billion of that aggregate revenue. Elevating coffee to an AU strategic status directly tackles this disparity, and our new Addis Ababa Office at the African Union will serve as the strategic operational backbone to make this happen." Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Ambassador Rutega said a central pillar of the joint AU-IACO strategy is a major push for industrial value addition, shifting decisively from exporting raw green coffee beans to locally processed, roasted, and packaged products. He noted that domestic processing increases coffee's economic value exponentially--from roughly $2 per kilogram of raw beans to up to $40 per kilogram of finished product--directly securing the livelihoods of over 10 million households across Africa. In response, Kafeero commended IACO's leadership and reaffirmed Uganda's steadfast commitment to the initiative. "Uganda fully embraces the opening of the new IACO office here in Addis Ababa, which will undoubtedly accelerate our regional trade ambitions under the African Continental Free Trade Area," she remarked. "By leveraging an integrated 1.5 billion consumer market, we can successfully bypass traditional global supply chains that have historically disproportionately rewarded international brokers." Kafeero also highlighted the critical leadership roles of the continent's major coffee powers. "Africa accounts for roughly 12% of worldwide production, heavily anchored by two dominant producers. Ethiopia stands as the biological birthplace of Arabica coffee, contributing roughly 39% of the continent's output. Side by side, Uganda stands proud as Africa's premier exporter and rapidly growing producer specializing in high-yield Robusta, accounting for 23% of total production. Together, our nations are vital to steering this framework toward success." Thursday, October 29, 2026 Sign in / Join Facebook Instagram Linkedin Mail Spotify X Youtube Nigeria Africa World Business and Tech Politics Sports Languages Yoruba Igbo Hausa French Arabic Fulfulde Kiswahili Mandarin connect Search Home Africa UN Political Mission Ends in Somalia After Three Decades Africa UN Political Mission Ends in Somalia After Three Decades October 29, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp The United Nations’ (UN) political mission in Somalia is scheduled to end on Saturday, closing more than three decades of successive UN political engagements aimed at supporting reconciliation, institution-building and political stability in the country. The closure follows a request by the Somali Government in 2024 and a UN Security Council-approved two-year transition of the mission’s responsibilities to Somali institutions and other UN bodies. The Somali Government has described the closure as a milestone in the country’s ability to manage its own affairs. However, opposition figures and analysts have raised concerns about the timing, citing political disagreements, continued militant attacks and growing humanitarian needs linked to drought. The departing United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia has advised political leaders and supported efforts to resolve disputes. Although the political mission is ending, African Union troops will continue to support Somali security forces in operations against militants, while UN humanitarian agencies will remain active in the country. READ ALSO: Somalia Announces Election Schedule A separate UN office will also continue providing logistical support, including supplies and transport, to African Union troops and some Somali security units. Decades of International Support Somalia’s central government collapsed in 1991 following the overthrow of President Mohamed Siad Barre, triggering years of conflict among rival factions and worsening humanitarian conditions. In 1992, the United States launched Operation Restore Hope to protect humanitarian relief deliveries during a famine. The following year, 18 American soldiers were killed during the Battle of Mogadishu, contributing to the end of the US military mission. UN peacekeepers withdrew in March 1995 without securing a lasting political settlement. The organisation subsequently established a civilian political office to support reconciliation. The office contributed to efforts that ended Somalia’s formal transitional period in 2012, when the country adopted a provisional constitution, established a new federal parliament and elected a president. Continued Support for Political Institutions Successive UN political missions have supported elections, justice institutions and regional administrations operating within Somalia’s federal system. In 2016, a UN-supported regional team helped implement a ceasefire between forces from Puntland and Galmudug, two regional administrations in central Somalia. Despite progress in rebuilding public institutions, disagreements over political authority and challenges in extending government control across the country remain. The end of the political mission marks a change in the UN’s engagement with Somalia, while continued international support through humanitarian agencies and security arrangements is expected to remain part of efforts to promote stability and development. somalia.content: Somalia’s election dispute reaches Supreme Court amid deepening political crisis - The EastAfrican Today's Paper | Our Brands Home East Africa Southern Africa Central Africa West Africa North Africa World Africa Eastern Africa More ••• Sign in My Account Personal details Change password Purchases Sign out Search Home News East Africa Southern Africa Central Africa West Africa North Africa World Africa Eastern Africa Business & Tech Opinion Columnists Editorials Cartoon Guest Blogs Sustainability Innovation Health Climate Magazine Services Today's Paper Our Brands Somalia’s election dispute reaches Supreme Court amid deepening political crisis Thursday, October 29, 2026 - 4 min read Some opposition leaders have rejected Somalia's national election timetable. Photo credit: Shutterstock By Xinhua News agency Thank you for reading businessdailyafrica.com Show plans Somalia’s political crisis has deepened after opposition leaders challenged recent constitutional amendments in the Supreme Court and rejected the newly announced national election timetable. The legal challenge, led by former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and supported by prominent opposition figures and the administrations of the federal member states of Puntland and Jubaland, seeks to overturn steps taken to revise the country’s Provisional Constitution and challenge the 2027 national election timetable announced by the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission. Ahmed’s office confirmed that a formal petition challenging the constitutional amendments was filed on October 11 and the Supreme Court received it the following day. Related East Africa PRIME Somalia election timetable deepens political divisions Oct 16 - 4 min read East Africa PRIME Mogadishu and neighbours at odds over transition wrangles Aug 29 - 5 min read Ahmed has accused the government of bypassing established legal procedures to push through sweeping changes without the agreement of the country’s political stakeholders. He said the amendments should have followed the procedures outlined in Chapter 15 of the Provisional Constitution, including provisions safeguarding the independence of parliamentary and constitutional review bodies. Ahmed also rejected claims that the changes had secured national consensus and urged the Supreme Court to consider his petition impartially and in accordance with the constitution. The legal challenge has added to existing tensions between the government and opposition groups over constitutional revisions and the framework for the upcoming national elections. The administrations of Puntland and Jubaland have also opposed the amendments, widening the political rift with Mogadishu. Analysts said the court’s handling of the dispute could significantly influence the country’s political trajectory and determine whether key regional stakeholders accept the legitimacy of the upcoming electoral process. Farhan Issak Yusuf, deputy head of the Mogadishu-based think tank Somali Public Agenda, said the petition marked a significant new development in the ongoing dispute, with opposition leaders increasingly turning to state institutions, particularly the judiciary, to challenge contentious government decisions. “The legal challenge follows the Supreme Court’s reported annulment of the Galmudug State election results, highlighting the judiciary’s potential role in resolving political disputes, particularly those related to electoral processes,” Issak told Xinhua . The Office of the Solicitor General told Xinhua that it had formally filed an objection to the opposition’s petition, setting the stage for a procedural dispute before the court considers the substance of the constitutional challenge. Separately, former President Mohamed Abdullahi Farmaajo has rejected the newly announced electoral timetable, warning that proceeding without broad political consensus could trigger renewed conflict. Farmaajo criticised the electoral commission as a “one-sided” body, alleging that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud was unilaterally pushing ahead with the 2027 election schedule, without the support of opposition leaders or key federal member states. The legal viability of the opposition’s challenge to the constitutional amendments remains uncertain, with questions surrounding its legal standing, the court’s jurisdiction and procedural hurdles. Legal expert Yahye Mohamed questioned whether the opposition coalition had the legal standing to bring the case, arguing that it lacked formal recognition as a constitutional entity and that its members had not reached sufficient consensus to file the petition. Mohamed also questioned whether the Supreme Court was the appropriate forum for the dispute, noting that constitutional matters would ideally be handled by a specialised constitutional court, an institution Somalia currently lacks. The conflicting legal arguments have left the case’s future uncertain. Its immediate trajectory will depend on how the Supreme Court responds to the state’s objection and whether it determines that it has jurisdiction to hear the challenge. Amid mounting legal and political tensions, Mohamud has stepped up efforts to bridge the widening political divide, inviting opposition leaders to participate in national consultations on federal elections scheduled for November 14 to 18, according to an official statement from Villa Somalia. The proposed talks aim to bring key political stakeholders together to discuss federal electoral issues through consensus and compromise, the statement said. Yusuf said resolving political differences through national institutions rather than relying on external mediation was a positive development. “Ultimately, the willingness to trust the country’s institutions and resolve political differences through them is a welcome development. Not so long ago, disputes of this nature were often settled through other means, with solutions frequently emerging from outside Somalia,” he said. He added that the legal challenge and the planned consultations underscored the parallel judicial and political tracks through which Somalia’s electoral and constitutional disputes were being addressed. As Somalia navigates its current political crisis and debates the roadmap for the 2027 elections, its electoral history highlights the long-standing challenges of returning to universal suffrage. Somalia last held direct, one-person-one-vote elections in March 1969, shortly before a bloodless military coup later that year overthrew the government. In recent electoral cycles, including those in late 2016, early 2017 and May 2022, parliamentary and presidential elections were conducted through a complex system of indirect voting. Mark Townsend Bio Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Bluesky Email Comments A colonel from US special operations in Somalia with a soldier from a branch of the Somali army trained by US special forces, in Mogadishu in 2023. Jonathan Torgovnik/Getty Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs. Sign up for the free Mother Jones Daily . This story was originally published by the Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five meters from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia , never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river. “The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.” Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba. “The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.” “The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war.” Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab , the Islamist militants who control 30 percent of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets. The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in East Africa , in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians. The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital . Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponizing” a rapidly strengthening El Niño , forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month. “The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia. The aftermath of the 2023 El Niño in Beledweyne in central Somalia. The 2023 El Niño caused the worst floods ever seen in the country. Pinning the population—which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead. “The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source. When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people . Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas—conceived to mitigate civilian casualties—to inflict harm. During the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time.” Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies , said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process—using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.” US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations, or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.” Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño . Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night—when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.” Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023 : Her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater. “In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old. US defense officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern.” The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) , meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding.” An aerial view of the Juba River, close to the town of Kismayo. Michael Runkel/Getty Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on October 1, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000. Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland , is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half. His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not.” Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says. The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2 billion. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled. Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defenses deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient. “They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks. Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged—and seemingly indiscriminate—campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security.” Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets. Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said. Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.” Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal about 8 inches long into her backyard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter: “It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.” Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March.” The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on March 19, but no other data is provided. Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes. Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region. An estimated 6,000 people may have died in Kismayo’s displacement sites since the Trump administration ended USAID last year. Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43 percent increase on last year. David Sterman, analyst at the New America think tank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.” The US, however, said it publicized “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.” Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia. Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger . Those fleeing the Juba valley—local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape—say there is insufficient food to sustain them. Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 12 inches apart. Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family—like many—shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.” In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery. Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea. El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels,” warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine. Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40 percent this year. Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night. For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness. “She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 9 pounds. Three days later: 10 pounds. She survived. Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare, or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River—often the poorest—things are about to get much worse. Looking for news you can trust? The ministry identified the vessels as TCG Gökçeada and TCG Yıldırım but did not disclose the quantity or type of military equipment being transported. advertisements It also did not specify whether the supplies were intended for the Somali National Armed Forces or Turkish military personnel stationed in Somalia. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to continuing military cooperation aimed at improving the capabilities of Somalia’s armed forces and contributing to regional security and stability. Turkey is one of Somalia’s key military partners, providing training, equipment and technical assistance to Somali security forces. Ankara operates a major military training facility in Mogadishu, where Turkish instructors have trained Somali soldiers as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s defence capabilities. The two countries have also expanded their military relationship through defence and maritime security agreements aimed at improving Somalia’s capacity to protect its territorial waters and combat security threats. The planned deployment of the two warships comes as Somalia and Turkey continue to deepen their military partnership, including cooperation on training, maritime security and defence capacity-building. somalia.content: Deputy Prime Minister Oversees Ports Ministry Handover as Macalin Takes Office - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Politics Nationwide Deputy Prime Minister Oversees Ports Ministry Handover as Macalin Takes Office October 29, 2026 4 min read MOGADISHU , Second Deputy Prime Minister Jibril Abdirashid Haji Abdi presided over a handover ceremony at the Ministry of Ports and Maritime Transport this week, formally transferring responsibilities to the new minister, Abdulkadir Omar Macalin, and the acting minister, State Minister Abdulkadir Mohamed. According to a report on the ceremony, the Deputy Prime Minister said the government’s strategic plan gives significant weight to efforts to improve the administration and services of ports and maritime transport, in order to achieve sustainable development consistent with the interests and priorities of the Federal Republic of Somalia. He said the outgoing and incoming officials are expected to continue the ministry’s work, strengthening cooperation between government institutions and international partners. The Context of the Appointment The handover follows a period of political and procedural complexity. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Macalin’s appointment , Macalin was appointed on October 17 to fill the vacancy created when Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur was elected Speaker of the House of the People in August. Macalin is himself a federal lawmaker. That dual role has been a source of contention. The new constitution, which took effect in April, bars cabinet members from holding parliamentary seats, and a six-month transition period ended on October 14. Speaker Nur asked Macalin to choose between his seat and his cabinet post. During a parliamentary session, Macalin publicly agreed that he had relinquished his parliamentary membership. But the Justice Minister later argued that separating lawmakers from the cabinet would create a constitutional vacuum because the government lacks the enabling legislation to fill the posts. The handover ceremony does not resolve that legal dispute. It simply formalizes Macalin’s assumption of the ministry’s day-to-day responsibilities. The Ministry’s Portfolio The Ministry of Ports and Maritime Transport oversees Somalia’s port infrastructure and maritime policy, areas of growing strategic importance. The ministry’s portfolio includes oversight of the Mogadishu port and coordination with international partners on maritime security and fisheries. The vacancy coincided with a period of heightened activity in Somalia’s maritime sector, including the implementation of the defense and economic cooperation framework with Türkiye, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Türkiye-Somalia partnership . The new minister inherits a docket that demands immediate attention, including the ongoing dispute over port tariffs and the federal government’s efforts to harmonize customs revenue across competing ports. As reported in FTL Somalia’s analysis of the port tariff gap , the ministry is central to resolving a fiscal dispute that costs the federal government millions in lost revenue. Critical Note The handover ceremony is a procedural formality, but it closes a gap that had persisted for over two months. During that period, the ministry operated without a permanent minister, while decisions on port policy, maritime security, and the Türkiye partnership continued to be made. The delay was not unusual by Somali standards, but it was consequential for a sector that sits at the intersection of economic development, security, and international partnership. Macalin’s appointment carries a certain political symmetry. He lost the speakership to the man whose ministerial seat he now inherits. Whether this reflects a consolation arrangement or a genuine assessment of his qualifications is not evident from the public record. What is clear is that the Prime Minister’s Office has filled a vacancy that should not have remained open as long as it did. The more substantive test will be whether Macalin can advance the ministry’s agenda without the institutional momentum that Nur had built over his tenure. The ports and maritime sector is not a ceremonial portfolio. It requires coordination with international partners, management of competing regional interests, and a clear strategy for revenue collection and infrastructure development. The Deputy Prime Minister’s remarks at the handover were forward-looking, but they did not address the specific challenges the new minister will face. Regardless of the result, the U-15 team’s performance in Baku has been a positive story for Somali football. The challenge, as always, is sustainability.
